newsitem.title: USA: More Americans eating out, study finds.
newsitem.headline: More Americans eating out, study finds.

text.p: The number of Americans eating out is increasing, according to a government study released on Wednesday.

In the latest results of a survey of American eating habits, the U.S. Agriculture Department found in 1994-95 that 57 percent of Americans ate out on any given day, accounting for about half their daily calorie and fat intake on average.
By comparison, in 1977-78, 43 percent of Americans ate away from home, for just over 40 percent of daily calories and fat.

"Given the prevalence of two-career families, the lack of time available for home cooking, and the wide variety of choices available for meals away from home, the increase is not surprising," Catherine Woteki, acting undersecretary for Research, Education and Economics said in a statement.

Woteki said teen-age boys were most likely to eat away from home, while people over 60 were least likely. On a typical day, over 70 percent of male teen-agers ate out against less than 40 percent of men and women at retirement age.

Among other trends pinpointed by the study: diners increasingly shun sit-down restaurants for fast-food places, men are more likely to eat out, and more whites (59 percent) dine out than blacks (51 percent).
Department nutritionist Lori Borrud noted that the figures in the study were averages and that eating out could mean anything from buying a cup of coffee to having three full meals.
The Agriculture Department report was based on interviews with nearly 11,000 men, women and children of all ages across the country during 1994-95.
Other government data hs found U.S. households spent nearly 40 percent of their food money on meals out since the mid-1980's, up sharply from 20 percent in the early 1970's.
